Abstract:
<jats:p>The integration of collaborative robots into industrial environments requires rigorous safety validation under the Power and Force Limiting (PFL) regime. This review article systematically maps the technological and normative development of certified Pressure and Force Measurement Devices (PFMDs) and experimental biofidelic instruments for Physical Human–Robot Interaction (pHRI) between the years 2011 and 2026. A quantitative screening of 68 studies revealed a publication peak in impact metrology in 2021. This peak occurred with a five-year latency after the release of the ISO/TS 15066 technical specification. Although global interest in collaborative robotics steadily grows, the publication trend indicates a gradual shift in scientific focus from reactive testing toward proactive prevention. A methodological deconstruction of four Research Questions (RQs) identifies persistent limitations in safety evaluation. The findings demonstrate that the internal structure of conventional sensors induces nonlinear shock filtering and parasitic oscillations (RQ1). Furthermore, the rigid fixation of test stands generates unrealistic pressure spikes. This physical limitation forces a transition to flexible and pendulum-based configurations (RQ2). Commercial flat films physically fail due to sensor saturation and introduced stiffness. Such failures accelerate the development of conformable electronic skins (e-skins) and multimodal test manikins (RQ3). To ensure interlaboratory reproducibility within the current ISO 10218-2:2025 standard, the text defines imperative metrological parameters. These parameters strictly include frequency response, calibration protocols, and volumetric mapping of inertial masses (RQ4). Furthermore, the analysed publications were systematically stratified into distinct technological categories, strictly reflecting their primary engineering domains, ranging from empirical metrological evaluation and sensor hardware design to advanced numerical modeling. Finally, the vision for future research anticipates a definitive shift toward proactive anti-collision technologies, encompassing Artificial Intelligence (AI), machine vision, and Augmented Reality/Virtual Reality/Mixed reality (AR/VR/MR). Future methodologies must also consider demographic anisotropies and the cognitive fatigue of the human operator.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Human–robot collaboration offers new opportunities to increase productivity, flexibility and ergonomics in work processes, however, it also introduces specific risks associated with a shared workspace between humans and robots, for which traditional risk assessment techniques may not be sufficiently effective. This article summarizes selected risk assessment techniques designed for the field of Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) and evaluates their strengths and weaknesses with respect to their applicability in a collaborative environment. Based on the identified limitations, a new hybrid technique is presented that combines Hierarchical Task Analysis (HTA), Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), Process Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (HRC–PFMEA) and Risk matrix. The proposed approach integrates qualitative and quantitative risk assessments, enables risk identification at an early stage of system design, and increases the transparency of work processes. The applicability and logical workflow of the proposed method are demonstrated using a simulation scenario of an assisted assembly workstation created in a digital environment.</jats:p>

## 5. Engineering Dignity: A Design Framework for Ethics, Affect and Agency in Human-Robot Collaboration

Abstract:
<jats:p>Collaborative robots have left the safety cage. In factories, operating theatres and care homes they now share physical and decision space with people. Physical safety is only one part of the ethical problem raised by that proximity. A second part concerns whether the person working beside the robot can still experience themselves as capable, recognised and in control of what they do. The question gains weight as robots become stronger and more precise, and as the AI systems directing them match or exceed human performance in narrow tasks and, plausibly, in broader ones. Technical standards such as ISO 10218:2025, which absorbs the former ISO/TS 15066, regulate force, speed and separation. The EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689) imposes human oversight obligations on high-risk systems. Neither instrument treats human dignity as a design property that can be specified, observed and audited, and neither addresses the risk that a more competent AI system diminishes human standing through cognitive rather than physical superiority. This paper proposes Dignity-by-Design (DbD), a framework that translates dignity-related concerns in robot ethics, drawing on Riek and Howard, on Sharkey and Sharkey, and on Nussbaum’s capabilities approach, into four operational principles: Informed Engagement, Override and Recovery, Affective Transparency, and Contextual Autonomy. Each principle carries auditable indicators, is anchored in Value Sensitive Design and is aligned with Article 14 of the AI Act. We work the framework through three deployment scenarios: an industrial cobot bench, an assistive robot for older adults, and an AI-supported professional decision environment. A research and certification roadmap follows, organised around a Dignity Impact Assessment. The contribution is conceptual rather than empirical. It offers a vocabulary and a measurement scaffold for moving dignity, as safety once moved, from ethical aspiration into engineering practice.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The growing need for sustainable and flexible automation solutions has led to the exploration of transforming traditional industrial robots into collaborative robots (cobots). This paper presents a framework for the conversion of conventional industrial robots into safe, intelligent, and sustainable cobots, leveraging advancements in artificial intelligence and computer vision and the principles of the circular economy. The proposed modular framework contains key components such as visual perception, cognitive adaptability, safe human–robot interactions, and reinforcement learning-based decision-making. Our methodology includes a comprehensive analysis of safety standards (e.g., ISO/TS 15066), robot typologies suitable for retrofitting, and sustainability strategies, including remanufacturing and lifecycle extension. A multi-phase implementation approach is laid out for a theoretical design to contribute to the development of cost-effective and environmentally responsible robotic systems, offering a scalable solution for extending the usability and social acceptance of legacy robotic platforms in collaborative settings.

Abstract:
<jats:p>What is considered safe for a robot operator during physical human–robot collaboration (HRC) is specified in corresponding HRC standards (e.g., ISO 10218‐2:2025). The regime that allows collisions between the moving robot and the operator, called Power and Force Limiting (PFL), restricts the permissible contact forces. Using the same fixed contact thresholds on the entire robot surface results unnecessary productivity losses, as the robot needs to stop even when impact forces are within limits. Here we present a framework that decides whether the robot should interrupt motion based on estimated collision force computed individually for different parts of the robot body and dynamically on the fly, based on the Effective Mass (EM) of each robot link. We performed experiments on a simulated and real collaborative robot arm (UR10e) with sensitive skin (AIRSKIN) for collision detection and isolation. To demonstrate the generality of our method, we added experiments on simulated KUKA LBR iiwa robot, where collision sensing draws on joint torque sensing. On a mock pick‐and‐place scenario with both transient and quasi‐static collisions, we show an increase in productivity over 45% from using the standard approach. The method is applicable to any robot for which the EF can be calculated.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>As humanoid robots move from controlled industrial environments into everyday human life, their safe integration is essential for societal acceptance and effective human–robot interaction (HRI). This scoping review examines engineering safety frameworks for humanoid robots across four core domains: (1) physical safety in HRI, (2) cybersecurity and software robustness, (3) safety standards and regulatory frameworks, and (4) ethical and societal implications. In the area of physical safety, recent research trends emphasize proactive, multimodal perception-based collision avoidance, the use of compliance mechanisms, and fault-tolerant control to handle hardware failures and falls. In cybersecurity and software robustness, studies increasingly address the full threat landscape, secure real-time communication, and reliability of artificial intelligence (AI)-based control. The analysis of standards and regulations reveals a lag between technological advances and the adaptation of key safety standards in current research. Ethical and societal studies show that safety is also shaped by user trust, perceived safety, and data protection. Within the corpus of 121 peer-reviewed studies published between 2021 and 2025 and included in this review, most work concentrates on physical safety, while cybersecurity, standardization, and socio-ethical aspects are addressed less frequently. These gaps point to the need for more integrated, cross-domain approaches to safety engineering for humanoid robots.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Research organizations and academics often seek to map the development of scientific fields, identify research gaps, and guide the direction of future research. In cobot-related research, the scientific literature consulted does not propose any comprehensive research agenda. Moreover, cobots, industrial robots inherently designed to collaborate with humans, bring with them emerging issues. To solve them, interdisciplinary research is often essential (e.g., combination of engineering, ergonomics and biomechanics expertise to handle safety challenges). This paper proposes an exhaustive study that employs a scoping review and bibliometric analysis to provide a structured macro perspective on the developments, key topics, and trends in cobot research for industry. A total of 2,195 scientific publications were gained from the Web of Science database, and a thorough selection process narrowed them down to 532 papers for comprehensive analysis. Descriptive statistics were employed to analyze bibliometric measures, highlighting publication trends, leading journals, the most productive institutions, engaged countries, influential authors, and prominent research topics. Co-authorship and bibliographic couplings were also examined. Through a co-occurrence analysis of terms, the content and research objectives of the papers were systematically reviewed and lead to a univocal categorization framework. That categorization can support organizations or researchers in different cobotics (collaborative robotics) fields by understanding research developments and trends, identifying collaboration opportunities, selecting suitable publication venues, advancing the theoretical and experimental understanding of automatic collaborative systems, and identifying research directions and predicting the evolution of publication quantity in cobotics.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Humanoid robots are increasingly tested in manufacturing and logistics, but technical demonstrations and shipment growth give an incomplete picture of deployment readiness. This paper examines the evidence needed to connect embodied capabilities with repeatable industrial operation. A focused narrative review draws on primary robotics studies, official industrial statistics, standards, and customer disclosures available through September 2026. It distinguishes demonstrated capability, task repeatability, integrated operation, and deployment transfer. The paper then develops an autonomy-adjusted cost model linking utilization, availability, relative task rate, autonomous first-pass yield, and supervision cost. A hypothetical sensitivity analysis shows how these factors jointly determine cost per autonomously accepted task. Under the stated assumptions, raising availability from 0.80 to 0.95 reduces the normalized cost from 1.111 to 0.936. Raising autonomous first-pass yield from 0.90 to 0.99 alone leaves the ratio at 1.010. These calculations describe model behavior and do not estimate commercial performance. Published factory disclosures show repeated execution of defined tasks but leave intervention rates and comparable operating costs unresolved. The paper provides a framework for interpreting deployment evidence and a proposed field evaluation protocol. The protocol is designed to test whether humanoid systems can sustain acceptable output across shifts, task variants, and sites.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Working in an academic laboratory (lab) often involves handling hazardous substances (Shariff & Norazahar,
2012). These substances are dangerous due to their toxic, flammable, explosive, carcinogenic, pathogenic or
radioactive properties (Furr, 2000). Therefore, it is crucial that those working in these environments do so safely.
Recently, many researchers and students from various universities in the U.S. and globally have suffered severe
injuries and fatalities from lab accidents. For example, in 2008 a lab fire at the University of California Los Angeles
led to the death of a student(Van Noorden, 2011). Following this and other similar accidents that transpired
afterwards, an international study was conducted to understand the state of safety within the wet labs of today’s
universities(Van Noorden, 2013a). The findings revealed numerous safety gaps and an overall lack of a strong and
positive safety culture within the labs (Benderly, 2013;and Schröder, Huang, Ellis, Gibson, & Wayne, 2016).

Since the majority of the accidents and study reports were predominantly from the U.S., it is unknown if the
same safety gaps and risks also exist in the wet labs of Canadian universities. Therefore, this research study
examined the state of safety within the wet laboratories of a medium-sized Canadian university. This was achieved
by: 1) conducting an inventory of the labs’ hazardous substances to identify their labeling and storage conditions, 2)
inspecting the labs to identify potential hazards or risky conditions, and 3) surveying lab personnel to understand
how safety is perceived and practiced. The results show several safety deficiencies and a negative perception on
certain safety elements among the lab personnel. As in universities in the U.S. there is an overall need to enhance thecurrent culture of safety at this Canadian university.

Abstract:
The assessment of the explosibility and severity characteristics of Bayan coal and Tanito coal was investigated over various concentrations in a 20 L Siwek spherical explosion chamber. The coals tested in this study were also compared with other organic dusts such as palm‐based soap noodle, tea powder, black rice, and rice flour, which were tested using the same explosion chamber and procedures. The severity and explosibility of the coals increase as their concentration increases. The Pmax of Bayan coal (10.15 bar) is higher than that of Tanito coal (7.35 bar). The Kst of Bayan coal (48.04 bar m s−1) is also higher than that of Tanito coal (16.83 bar m s−1). Among all the dusts studied using the same chamber and procedures, palm‐based soap noodle has the highest Pmax at 16 bar, while tea powder has the lowest Pmax at 6.35 bar. The results show that the explosibility and severity of the coals increase as the concentrations increase, and the moisture content, coal ranking, and different types of organic dust have a significant influence on the severity characteristics of dust explosions.

Abstract:
In the realm of Industry 4.0, diverse technologies such as AI, Cyber-Physical Systems, IoT, and advanced sensors converge to shape smarter future factories. Mobile manipulators (MMs) are pivotal, fostering flexibility, adaptability, and collaboration in industrial processes. On one hand, MMs offer a remarkable level of flexibility, adaptability, and collaboration in industrial processes, facilitating swift production line changes and efficiency enhancements. On the other hand, their integration into real manufacturing environments requires meticulous considerations, such as safety, human–robot interaction, and cybersecurity. This article delves into MMs’ essential role in achieving Industry 4.0’s automation and adaptability by integrating mobility with manipulation capabilities. The study reviews MMs’ industrial applications and integration into manufacturing systems. The most observed applications are logistics (49%) and manufacturing (33%). As Industry 4.0 advances, the paper emphasizes updating and aligning MMs with the smart factory concept by networks of sensors and the real-time analysis of them, especially for an enhanced human–robot interaction. Another objective is categorizing considerations for MMs’ utilization in Industry 4.0-aligned manufacturing. This review methodically covers a wide range of considerations and evaluates existing solutions. It shows a more comprehensive approach to understanding MMs in Industry 4.0 than previous works. Key focus areas encompass perception, data analysis, connectivity, human–robot interaction, safety, virtualization, and cybersecurity. By bringing together different aspects, this research emphasizes a more integrated view of the role and challenges of MMs in the Industry 4.0 paradigm and provides insights into aspects often overlooked. A detailed and synthetic analysis of existing knowledge was performed, and insights into their future path in Industry 4.0 environments were provided as part of the contributions of this paper. The article also appraises initiatives in these domains, along with a succinct technology readiness analysis. To sum up, this study highlights MMs’ pivotal role in Industry 4.0, encompassing their influence on adaptability, automation, and efficiency.

Abstract:
Digital Twins (DTs) are transforming manufacturing by bridging the physical and digital worlds, enabling real-time insights, predictive analytics, and enhanced decision making. In Industry 4.0, DTs facilitate automation and data integration, while Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-centric, resilient, and sustainable production. However, implementing DTs in robotic metal additive manufacturing (AM) remains challenging because of the complexity of the wire-based laser metal deposition (LMD) process, the need for real-time monitoring, and the demand for advanced defect detection to ensure high-quality prints. This work proposes a structured DT architecture for a robotic wire-based LMD cell, following a standard framework. Three DT implementations were developed. First, a real-time 3D simulation in RoboDK, integrated with a 2D Node-RED dashboard, enabled motion validation and live process monitoring via MQTT (message queuing telemetry transport) telemetry, minimizing toolpath errors and collisions. Second, an Industrial IoT-based system using KUKA iiQoT (Industrial Internet of Things Quality of Things) facilitated predictive maintenance by analyzing motor loads, joint temperatures, and energy consumption, allowing early anomaly detection and reducing unplanned downtime. Third, the Meltio dashboard provided real-time insights into the laser temperature, wire tension, and deposition accuracy, ensuring adaptive control based on live telemetry. Additionally, a prescriptive analytics layer leveraging historical data in FireStore was integrated to optimize the process performance, enabling data-driven decision making.

                             Abstract

Explosion venting is a critical passive protection strategy for industrial systems handling
combustible dust, flammable gases, and hybrid vapors. Despite established standards,
recent incidents such as the 2025 biomass facility explosion in Fremont, Nebraska highlight
a persistent gap between theoretical design and field performance. This paper examines the
fundamentals of NFPA 68 (2023), bridging combustion thermodynamics and  fluid
dynamics with practical engineering.

Special focus is directed toward Chapter 7, "Venting Deflagrations of Gas Mixtures and
Mists," providing a technical deconstruction of optimal vent sizing. The analysis details
critical parameters including the deflagration index (KSt), maximum explosion pressure
(Pmax), target reduced pressure (Pred), and the turbulent flame enhancement factor (λ). A
case study involving cyclohexane (CHX) off-gassing in legacy rundown silos illustrates
how partial volumes, mixture leanness, turbulence, and geometric constraints dictate
required vent areas.

Additionally, this paper addresses the limitations of empirical correlations regarding
length-to-diameter (L/D) ratios and hybrid mixture complexities. It concludes by exploring
the transition to NFPA 660 (2025), emphasizing that modern process engineers must move
beyond rote calculation toward integrated explosion protection strategies that combine
conservative design, material testing, and dynamic modeling.
1  Introduction

Combustible dust, flammable gases, and hybrid mixture explosions continue to pose an
omnipresent threat to the global process, chemical, and manufacturing industries. From
agricultural grain handling and biomass storage to advanced pharmaceutical manufacturing
and petrochemical synthesis, the fundamental risk of a deflagration wave propagating
through a confined, unburned fuel-air mixture is a ubiquitous operational hazard. WhenGCPS 2026
________________________________________________________________________

these  inevitable  ignition events occur within  the  restrictive boundaries of process
enclosures such as silos, dust collectors, bucket elevators, and reactors, the resulting
isochoric (constant volume) pressure rise can rapidly exceed the mechanical structural
design limits of the equipment. Without the adequate and rapid deployment of mitigation
systems, this sudden overpressure leads to catastrophic vessel rupture, hazardous high-
velocity fragmentation, widespread structural collapse, and tragic loss of human life.

The stark reality of these operational hazards was recently underscored by the explosion
and subsequent fires at the Horizon Biofuels facility in Fremont, Nebraska, on July 29,
2025. (1,2) This catastrophic incident, which claimed the lives of a facility operator and his
two young daughters who were on-site, serves as a sobering reminder of the destructive
potential of combustible particulates. Preliminary investigations conducted by the U.S.
Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) and the Nebraska State Fire
Marshal's office quickly pointed to a combustible wood dust explosion—a widely
recognized, heavily documented, yet entirely avoidable hazard within the domestic wood
processing and biomass energy sectors. (1,2) The incident was characterized by a sudden
localized release of dust and smoke from a processing tower, which was followed almost
instantaneously by a massive secondary blast that collapsed the building and trapped the
victims inside.  (2) The Horizon Biofuels tragedy perfectly exemplifies the catastrophic
nature of secondary  dust  explosions, wherein an  initial,  relatively minor primary
deflagration generates a pressure wave that accumulates fugitive dust into suspension,
providing an optimal fuel cloud for a devastating subsequent blast. (3)

To mitigate such catastrophic overpressures, the NFPA published and continually refines
Standard 68, Standard on Explosion Protection by Deflagration Venting, which serves as
the  preeminent  scientifically  grounded  global  benchmark  for  designing  passive
deflagration  relief systems. The premise of NFPA 68  is straightforward: provide a
sacrificial, deliberately weak structural element (the explosion vent panel or door) that is
engineered to physically open at a predetermined static activation pressure (Pstat). The
deployment of this closure provides a relief area that allows the violently expanding
fireball, unburned fuel, and high-pressure combustion gases to rapidly escape into the
outside atmosphere or a designated safe area. By doing so, the system limits the maximum
internal pressure of the process vessel to a pre-calculated safe level known as the reduced
pressure (Pred). (4)

However, the conceptual simplicity of installing an explosion vent often dangerously
masks the mathematical, kinetic, and thermodynamic complexity of its actual application.
Many engineering practitioners inadvertently treat NFPA 68 as a simple collection of
"plug-and-play" algebraic equations, simply inputting volumes and material indices while
neglecting the critical boundary conditions such as internal fluid turbulence, complex
vessel geometries, partial volume effects, acoustic instabilities, and vent duct aerodynamic
back pressure that defines the validity of these mathematical models.

This paper aims to deconstruct these underlying complexities. By systematically reviewing
the recently updated 2023 edition of NFPA 68 and analyzing a nuanced real-world process
safety case study involving CHX hydrocarbon off-gassing in polymer processing silos, this
analysis will demonstrate that effective, compliant, and safe venting design requires notGCPS 2026
________________________________________________________________________

merely mathematical rigor, but sound engineering judgment rooted in a deep understanding
of combustion science. (5,6)
2 The Physics of Deflagration and Combustion Dynamics

Before engaging with the specific algebraic sizing methodologies prescribed by NFPA 68,
it is essential to establish an understanding of the underlying combustion physics that
govern deflagrations. First published in 1945 as a relatively rudimentary "Guide for
Venting of Deflagrations," the standard has evolved through eight decades of empirical
testing, catastrophic incident reviews, and fundamental thermodynamic research. The 2023
edition organizes venting methodologies based primarily on the physical state and phase
of the combustible fuel, recognizing that solid dust clouds, liquid mists, and gas vapors
burn with different chemical kinetic behaviors. (4)

NFPA 68 formally defines combustible dust as a finely divided combustible particulate
solid encompassing combustible fibers and flyings that present a flash-fire hazard or a
severe explosion hazard when suspended in air, or another process-specific oxidizing
medium, over a specific range of fuel-to-air concentrations. A classical dust explosion is
initiated when these highly fine combustible particles are dispersed and suspended in a
confined space, forming a localized cloud, and are subsequently exposed to an ignition
source possessing sufficient thermal energy (such as an electrostatic discharge spark,
frictional heating, or a hot mechanical surface). Unlike a simple smoldering fire or a liquid
pool fire, which relies entirely on slow surface vapor diffusion, a suspended dust cloud
allows for exceptionally rapid volumetric combustion. The finer the particulate matter, the
higher its specific surface area

severe explosion hazard when suspended in air, or another process-specific oxidizing

allows for exceptionally rapid volumetric combustion. The finer the particulate matter, the
higher its specific surface area relative to its mass. This increased surface area facilitates
overwhelmingly faster radiative heat transfer and chemical devolatilization, resulting in an
almost instantaneous ignition sequence and the generation of a high-velocity flash fire. (3,6)

When this reactive combustion zone referred to as the flame front propagates through the
unreacted, suspended fuel-air medium at a velocity that is less than the local speed of sound
in that unreacted medium, the thermodynamic phenomenon is formally classified as a
deflagration. In a deflagration, the pressure wave travels ahead of the flame front, pre-
compressing the unburned fuel. In contrast, if the combustion wave physically couples with
a shockwave and accelerates to exceed the local speed of sound, it abruptly transitions into
detonation. In a detonation regime, traditional explosion venting  is rendered largely
ineffective, if not entirely useless, due to the microsecond timescales of the pressure spike,
which destroy the vessel before the mechanical vent panel can overcome its own inertia.
(5,6)

Deflagration venting therefore relies on the critical assumption that the flame front remains
subsonic. This allows the rapidly expanding hot burned gases to push the unburned mixture
ahead of it, eventually exerting sufficient mechanical force to burst the vent panel and
relieve the internal pressure well before the vessel's ultimate tensile structural strength is
breached. Understanding this fundamental difference is what drives the strict geometric
and kinetic limitations codified within NFPA 68.GCPS 2026

3  Fundamentals of Deflagration Venting (NFPA 68)

To accurately engineer a functional, reliable, and compliant explosion vent, a process
safety practitioner must master specific nomenclature and a complex set of thermodynamic
parameters that quantitatively describe the severity of the anticipated explosion. Chapter 6
of NFPA 68, titled “Fundamentals of Venting of Deflagrations,” provides the foundational
mathematical and physical framework for these parameters, bridging the gap between
small-scale laboratory testing and massive industrial equipment. (4)

3.1 Deflagration Index (K)

The single most critical kinetic parameter governing the entire vent sizing calculation is
the deflagration index, denoted universally as K. This index is a mathematically normalized
metric of the maximum rate of pressure rise attained by an optimally mixed combustible
fuel-air mixture ignited in a closed spherical test vessel of a known volume, V. Because
the surface area of a spherically expanding flame front dictates the rate of heat release, and
geometric volume scales differently than surface area, the overall pressure rise rate is
normalized using the cubic law to allow for scale-up to larger industrial vessels. The
fundamental equation is defined as below:

                    K= (dP/dt)max * V1/3

successfully relieve the dynamic pressure before catastrophic structural failure occurs. (4)

3.2 Maximum Explosion Pressure (Pmax)

Pmax is defined as the maximum or gauge pressure developed in a fully contained, unvented
deflagration of an optimally concentrated (typically slightly fuel-rich or stoichiometric)
mixture, assuming the vessel is entirely closed, and no explosion panels, relief valves, or
structural leakages exist to relieve the pressure. (4) It represents the thermodynamic upper
limit of the explosion's destructive capability.

For combustible dust, both KSt and Pmax must be empirically determined through highly
controlled, standardized, and repeatable laboratory testing. These tests are exclusively
conducted in heavily calibrated, near-spherical stainless steel test vessels of at least 20 liters
in volumetric capacity, adhering to international protocols such as ASTM E1226, Standard
Test Method for Explosibility of Dust Clouds. The 20-liter sphere utilizes precisely timed
chemical igniters and highly sensitive, flush-mounted piezoelectric pressure transducers
coated in silicone rubber to minimize thermal shock, ensuring calibration stability during
the milliseconds of the explosion. (7)

However, owing to the significantly more uniform mixing characteristics, molecular
diffusion rates, and different flame wrinkling dynamics of gaseous vapors, flammable
gases are typically tested to determine Pmax in a specifically designed test vessel of at least
5 liters in capacity, though larger vessels are often employed to mitigate wall-quenching
effects. (4,6)

3.3 Reduced Pressure (Pred)

Pred is defined as the maximum pressure developed within a vented process enclosure
during the actual course of a vented deflagration event. (4)

Regardless of the fuel type, be it a complex pharmaceutical powder, agricultural grain, or
volatile hydrocarbon gas, the overarching engineering design objective remains identical:
ensuring that the reduced pressure (Pred) does not exceed two-thirds of the ultimate yield
strength of the specific enclosure (or the specific yield stress, depending precisely on the
permissible deformation limits established by the facility's mechanical integrity program)
(4,6). If a facility accepts that a silo may bulge but not burst during an explosion, the target
Pred may be set slightly higher, allowing for a smaller, more economical vent panel. If zeroGCPS 2026
________________________________________________________________________

deformation is the mandate, Pred must be set exceptionally low, which might require larger
venting areas.


3.4 Static Activation Pressure (Pstat)

The static activation pressure, universally denoted as Pstat, is the mechanically defined
pressure differential at which the physical vent closure (such as a rupture panel or explosion
door) yields, bursts, shears its retaining pins, or opens when exposed to a sudden internal
pressure spike. (4)

The relationship between Pstat and Pred is critical and heavily regulated within the standard.
NFPA 68 dictates that the value of Pstat shall not exceed two-thirds of Pred. This requirement
guarantees that the vent panel opens early enough in the steep pressure-time curve to
establish a full volumetric discharge flow before the peak combustion pressure is ever
reached. A delayed vent opening caused either by a Pstat set too high or by a vent panel
possessing  excessive  physical  mass  will  result  in  catastrophic  internal  pressure
accumulation.

A Chavan. Venting the blast-nfpa 68 fundamentals, design guidance and limitations, and real-world challenges for modern process safety. Unknown journal, 2026.

The excerpt contains the relevant paragraph stating that NFPA 660 was officially issued in 2025 and consolidates the six legacy combustible-dust standards into one unified document. The surrounding text specifically identifies NFPA 652 (Fundamentals of Combustible Dust) and NFPA 484 (Metals) among the previously applicable standards that facilities had to navigate. The most direct supporting passage begins with “Historically, combustible dust regulations were heavily fragmented” and explains that facilities previously used NFPA 652 together with commodity-specific standards such as NFPA 484, NFPA 61, and NFPA 654; it then states that NFPA 660 consolidates all six legacy standards. However, this excerpt does not explicitly use the word “supersedes,” nor does it state an “applicable jurisdiction code.” It only says that NFPA 660 was issued in 2025 and consolidated the legacy standards. Therefore, the excerpt can support the combination/consolidation claim, but not a precise claim about supersession or jurisdictional applicability.

                    ABSTRACT

    his article describes several aspects of oxygen (O2) deficiency with an emphasis on respirator
   programs and respirator selection. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration’s (OSHA) 29T  CFR 1910.1341 and ANSI/ASSE Z88.2-2015 (Z88.2) have much  in common.  However,  their
exposure criteria and terminology used for describing levels of O2-deficiency and the approaches to
assessing O2-deficiency  differ.  These differences can have a significant impact on an employer’s
respirator program and respirator selections for workplaces at altitudes above sea level.

       Under certain circumstances, Z88.2 leads to a more conservative respirator selection than OSHA
because its O2-deficiency criteria and hazard assessment approach relies directly on partial pressure of
oxygen (PO2)2 at all altitudes. Z88.2 defines an O2-deficient atmosphere as either immediately dangerous
to life or health (IDLH), or non-IDLH based on the atmosphere’s PO2 and defines respirator selection for
these two O2-deficient atmospheres.  Unlike Z88.2, OSHA does not directly access the biologically
significant aspect of an atmosphere’s PO2 in its hazard assessment. OSHA defines an O2-deficient
atmosphere based upon a percentage of oxygen. OSHA does not use the term “O2-deficient IDLH”;
however, OSHA considers any atmosphere with less than 19.5% O2 as IDLH and defines respirator
selection for IDLH atmospheres.  Although OSHA does not use the term “PO2” in their respirator
standard, OSHA’s exceptions to O2-deficient IDLH respirator selection policy are based on PO2 altitude-
adjusted, O2 percentage criteria.

        This article provides descriptions of OSHA and Z88.2 requirements to evaluate workplace oxygen
deficiency, their approaches to O2-deficiency hazard assessment, and describes their significance on
respirator programs and selections. Alternative solutions to wearing respirators for protection against O2-
deficiency resulting solely from high altitudes are also discussed.  Selection and implementation of
alternative solutions by the employer and their Physician or other Licensed Health Care Professional
(PLHCP) are not covered by either respirator standard.  Appendix A provides information about the

Understanding Oxygen Deficiency

      Each year, many workers are injured or die due to O2-deficiency.  Bureau of Labor Statistics
(BLS, 2011) reported 62 and 60 occupational fatalities, respectively during the years 2009 and 2010 due
to O2-deficiency. One of the problems with O2-deficient atmospheres is that at lowered concentrations,
starting at approximately 16% O2 by volume, attentiveness and thinking becomes impaired.  This of
course, varies based on the individual’s fitness and acclimatization.  Individuals impaired by exposure to
deficient levels of O2 have died simply because they did not recognize the peril they were in, even though
they should have been able to easily escape from this hazard. There have been reports of workers who
have opened a hatch to an O2-deficient atmosphere and died with only their head inside the hazard. The
low level of O2 resulted in a feeling of euphoria and the workers could not comprehend that they only
needed to lean back out of the hatch to save their lives. From discussion with one of the original human
test subjects in an early study of hypoxia (Reinert, 2016), he knew that he was about to die and would
have allowed himself to die if he had not been in a controlled experiment. He explained that he was not
concerned about his imminent death because of the intense euphoric feeling experienced from breathing
low concentrations of oxygen.

                                                                        226.4 Mechanism of Injury and Symptoms


These interactions with biological tissue can be grouped into thermal, acoustical and photochemical
effects.

      Photo-Thermal Effects
Thermal effects occur when sufficient electromagnetic radiant energy from the laser beam has been
absorbed by the biological tissue and the molecules experience an increase in heat energy. This energy
can result in burn injury to a confined area extending further around the incident beam site with
increased time of exposure. Significant tissue injury can occur with only milliseconds of exposure.

      Photo-Mechanical Effects
Photo-mechanical or sometimes referred to as acoustical effects occur when a laser beam is incident
on the tissue which is heated very rapidly in only nanoseconds or less, inducing a mechanical
shockwave. Typically associated with very short pulses, less than nanoseconds, the liquid component
of the tissues may evaporate into a hot gas with extremely high temperatures. The phase changes are
so rapid that they are explosive and the cells rupture.

      Photo-Chemical Effects
Photochemical effects can be the direct result of specific wavelength absorption resulting in chemical
changes in exposed biological tissues, typically in the UV range. This photochemical reaction is
believed to be responsible for damage at relatively low levels of exposure where duration of exposure
is more significant. The skin, the cornea and the lens of the eye, may experience irreversible changes
induced by prolonged exposure to moderate levels of UV radiation. Such photochemical induced
changes may result in injury if the duration of irradiation is excessive, or if shorter exposures are
repeated over prolonged periods.

     Symptoms of Laser Induced Injury to the Eye
We have been discussing the mechanism of injury to the various parts of the eye but it is useful at this
stage to list the main symptoms you may experience if you are unfortunate enough to have a laser
beam induced injury to your eyes. Please note, it is important to understand that the apparent
absence of immediate symptoms does not mean that serious damage has not been done. You should
seek medical attention and report the incident.

   Headache shortly after exposure, excessive watering of the eyes, sudden appearance of
     floaters.
   Minor corneal burns cause a gritty feeling, like sand in the eye
   The exposure to a visible laser beam can be detected by a bright colour flash of the emitted
    wavelength and an after-image of its complementary colour (e.g., a green 532 nm laser light
    would produce a green flash followed by a red after-image).
   Exposure to near Infra-red beams are especially hazardous and it may initially go undetected
    because the beam is invisible and the retina lacks pain sensory nerves.
   Photo-Mechanical retinal damage may be associated with an audible "pop" at the time of
    exposure. Visual disorientation due to retinal damage may not be apparent to the operator until
     considerable thermal damage has occurred.

                                                                        379 CONTROLS AND PROTECTION
Wherever a risk of personal injury or possible damage to a working environment exists through the
use of lasers, control measures must be implemented. The degree of these measures may be
determined through an accurate risk assessment or directives from the LSO and recommendations
from the manufacturer. Risk should be completely removed or reduced to the absolute minimum
possible.

9.1  Hierarchy





The hierarchy for control measures shows the most preferable first with the least preferable at the
bottom. An example is given for each measure below.

       Elimination: remove the hazard completely, if you do not need a laser then remove it from
       the lab.
       Substitution: If you do not need the power of a CLASS 3B laser replace it with a CLASS 2 or
      3R
       Isolate: completely enclose the laser system so that no beam is accessible
       Engineering control: use interlocks on the enclosure or the entrance to the laser designated
       area
       Administrative control: Put appropriate signs on the door to alert people to the hazards and
         risks
       Personal protective equipment: Use the appropriate protective eyewear for the laser in use

This hierarchy is common for all risk management and can be applied to other secondary non-beam
dangers associated with laser systems. The first two on this list should be well considered before
commencing with a particular experimental setup. The last three will be dealt with here in a little more
detail as they deal with hazards that cannot be completely removed.





                                                                        389.2  Engineering


Engineering controls and measures are recognised as being far superior to administrative ones as they
help remove the human element and do not require a degree of compliance by the individual. Micro
switches and interlocks that shut the laser off when covers are removed or doors opened are much
more reliable than trusting people to follow procedure. In the R&D environment there are challenges
to implementing effective engineering controls that do not inhibit the functionality or the progress of
work. Very often decisions need to be made in conjunction with the LSO to reduce the risk as far as
possible using engineering controls and then augment with added administrative ones to help better
protect the users. For example, this could happen where there are multiple wavelengths in a laser
laboratory coming from the same or other laser systems. It may not be possible to interlock all
enclosures and screens around a particular system but by defining what eye protection must be worn
and where people are prohibited from in the room the risk can further reduce the risk.

      Use beam enclosures and place beam blocks and screens where possible.
       Block stray beams with beam blocks
      Reduce the power of the beam to as low as possible.
      Reduce the power of the beam during alignment procedures.
      Ensure all optical components and mounts are securely fixed
      Keep the beam below eye level and parallel with the surface of the optical bench.
      Use a Laser Designated Area (LDA) with interlocks.
       Provide good ventilation and extraction if required.
      Ensure there is no possibility of the beam escaping the LDA.





Screens can be used to surround an experimental setup to stop stray beams from exiting the optical
bench area. Tubes can be used in the experimental setup to enclose beams so that items cannot fall
into the beam path and accidently deflect the beam towards a person’s eyes. Beam blocks / dumps
may be needed where an optical component inadvertently splits the beam, e.g. cube polarisers,
diffraction gratings.

It is important to use non-flammable material when setting up screens and other enclosures. They can
be purchased commercially.

If it is possible, it is always ideal to enclose the laser system completely with a fully interlocked light
tight enclosure effectively reducing it to CLASS 1. It may also help to assist your experimental work by
blocking out the ambient light and help stabilise environmental effects such as temperature.





                                                                        399.3  Administrative
Administrative controls are next on the list in the hierarchy of control measures. They depend on the
people acting correctly on information and following work procedures. Their implementation and
effectiveness depends on the compliance of the laser users and others working in the vicinity.
Administrative controls cover the laser safety policies of the university, the implementation of the
laser safety management program, work procedures, training, registration and assignment of
responsibilities.





Administrative controls will consist mainly of the following

     Laser Safety Training and Registration.
     Laser Designated Areas with Warning Lights!
     Logging use of the laser
     Removal and return of the power supply keys to a designated point
     Good signage both the Lasers and entry points
     Risk assessment and Scheme of Work

As a laser user or if you work in the vicinity of active lasers you will be expected to comply with all
administrative controls put in place by your lab supervisor and LSO and to complete a risk assessment
appropriate for your laser system.


9.4  Personal Protection Equipment
The nature of the work involving Laser systems in the university environment means that it is not
always practical to reduce the danger of exposure to levels of artificial optical radiation to zero by
engineering control measures alone. Access to the beam for the servicing of the laser or setting up of
optical components and samples for analysis is often necessary as a matter of routine. Personal
protective equipment, (PPE) is required to ensure that in the event of an accidental exposure the laser
user is not injured.

Exposure of the skin to direct beams should always be avoided but in the case of the UV wavelengths

10 SELECTING LASER SAFETY EYEWEAR
Ultimately Laser Safety Eyewear is your last line of protection, it is the least preferable as it implies
that the hazard has not been completely removed or reduced to a safe level and you are therefore
potentially exposed and at risk of injury. Very often safety laser windows use the same filter materials
as do eyewear so the process of selecting the filter material is the same; both must comply with the
same European standards, EN207 and EN208.

Choosing the correct Laser Safety Eyewear to wear is not trivial and you must ensure that you are
competent enough to be able to select the correct eyewear for the laser beam you are working with.

Always check the eyewear you are using; do not assume just because it was handed to you or because
it was beside a laser that it is correct. Many laser systems are tuneable and can have their output
changed, power, wavelength, emission mode, repetition rate and pulse energy can be changed by the
user.

All laser safety eyewear must be cleaned and stored appropriately to help keep them in good
condition, do not use non-recommended solvents as they may affect the filters. Speak with the
manufacturer / supplier for details. Safety Eyewear should be placed in storage near the entry point
to the LDA so that they can be put on before entering.

Laser safety eyewear works by simply absorbing the laser light so that it does not reach your eyes. The
filter material and frame must be able to absorb the energy of a laser beam strike without losing
integrity.

When using EN207 and EN208 in most cases we do not need to worry about calculating the MPEs

It is important that you know how to choose and check the laser eye protection you are required to
wear for the laser system you are using. Do not rely on your colleagues to provide you with the correct
information you must be proficient in calculating and choosing the correct protection level for

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Hazard / subsystem | Evidence or design basis | Design-review proposal / acceptance criterion |
|---|---|---|
| **Laser enclosure / guard** | A historical IEC 60825-4 committee report suggested passive-guard test classes **T1 = 30,000 s**, **T2 = 100 s**, and **T3 = 10 s**; these are not universal guarantees under the current standard. Testing used worst-case credible exposure and required rear-side emission below the Class 1 AEL. At 500 W, the corresponding incident energies are **15 MJ, 50 kJ, and 5 kJ**. No blanket survivability time for aluminium or steel sheet follows from these values. (pqac-00000022) | Make normal operation **Class 1** by validated enclosure testing. Use a two-channel monitored, guard-locking interlock; safety shutter/attenuator; laser-source inhibit; scanner safe-torque-off; captured beam dump; and manual reset outside the hazard zone. Qualify every wall, seam, aperture, window, dump, and likely aluminium back-reflection path at worst-case focus, fault position, beam diameter, power, and response time. Treat service with containment defeated as **Class 4** under an LSO-approved SOP and NHZ. |
| **Oxygen / argon** | OSHA treats **<19.5% O₂** as oxygen-deficient/IDLH. A NIST LPBF installation warned below 19% and evacuated below 17%; it also recommended fixed room monitoring, argon shutoff, ventilation, and outdoor exhaust. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000065) | Install independent O₂ sensors in the room and inside the lift enclosure, positioned from a dispersion assessment—not merely “low because argon is heavy.” Proposed conservative controls: **warning at 20.0%**, automatic argon isolation and high ventilation no later than **19.5%**, and evacuation/latching alarm below 19.5%. Interlock laser and purge operation to ventilation and monitor health; provide pressure regulation, secured cylinders, check valves, relief devices, and safe outdoor discharge. |
| **Metal powders** | One AlSi10Mg test reported **Pmax 0.61 MPa (6.1 bar)**, **Kst 15.10 MPa·m/s (151 bar·m/s)**, and **MIE 80 mJ**; values depend strongly on particle-size distribution, oxidation, dispersion, and sample history. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000025, pqac-00000071) | Complete a combustible-dust DHA using representative virgin, reused, spilled, condensate, cyclone, and filter samples—not the published values alone. Minimize powder inventory and clouds; use conductive/bonded transfer paths, verified grounding, non-sparking tools, conductive footwear/flooring, closed containers, combustible-dust-rated vacuum equipment, exposure monitoring, and a medically managed respirator program. |
| **Cyclone / HEPA filter** | Cyclones enrich the downstream filter in finer dust. Filter-collected aluminium near **D50 ≈ 5 μm** has measured **MIE <3 mJ**, and filter Kst can be **2–3 times** that of bulk feed. Unpassivated LPBF condensate may ignite when air enters during maintenance. Wet systems suppress clouds but aluminium/water contact can generate hydrogen. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018) | Do not accept an ordinary HEPA unit as explosion protection. Use a metal-dust-qualified, process-specific inerted dry collector or engineered wet collector after compatibility review. Provide isolation, grounding, differential-pressure/temperature monitoring, safe venting or suppression where required, and an inert filter-change/passivation method. Filter changes require shutdown/LOTO, restricted access, two trained people, fire-resistant PPE, controlled air admission, and approved hazardous-waste packaging. |
| **Thermal / vacuum** | The proposed plate is **200 °C**, substantially hotter than the 80 °C NIST platform that required heat-resistant gloves. Pump-down to about 1 mbar exposes the chamber and viewport to essentially **one atmosphere differential pressure**; controlled-atmosphere window guidance requires design for maximum credible vacuum, fire, impact, deterioration, and positive pressure where applicable. (pqac-00000015, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044) | Guard and label accessible hot surfaces; use independent over-temperature sensing and a safety contactor, cooldown confirmation before robotic or manual exchange, heat-rated grippers, and a noncombustible landing station. Engineer the chamber, door, seals, and laser-rated viewport for full vacuum plus maximum positive pressure and faults; add protective retention/shielding, inspection criteria, vacuum/pressure relief, door pressure-equalization interlock, and proof documentation. |
| **Robot / mobile base / lift** | ISO 10218-1:2025 addresses robot design; ISO 10218-2:2025 addresses integrated applications/cells. ISO/TS 15066 supplies collaborative modes and contact criteria. ANSI/RIA R15.08 Part 1 covers mobile-robot manufacturers and Part 2 system integrators. “Cobot” status does not make the combined arm, payload, hot plate, drawer, machine, MiR, and lift application inherently safe. (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000059, pqac-00000062) | Perform one ISO 12100 lifecycle risk assessment covering docking error, dropped/hot loads, crushing and trapping, sharp parts, powder release, lift motion, unexpected restart, communications loss, and recovery/service. Require safety-rated docking and tray-position confirmation plus a **mobile interlock**: laser shutter closed and emission inhibited, chamber equalized/cool, lift and machine motion stopped, and robot/MiR in verified safe state before access. Coordinate E-stops and STO across all subsystems; validate stopping distances, payload/gripper retention, collaborative limits, reset locations, and prevention of automatic restart. |

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: A university research lab is designing a small laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine: a 500 W continuous-wave single-mode 1070 nm fiber laser (IPG YLR-500 class, Class 4) with a galvo scanner and f-theta lens over a 25 to 75 mm heated (200 C) build plate, in a sealed aluminium chamber that is pumped to about 1 mbar then held under argon at +5 to +20 mbar with O2 below 100 ppm, processing aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc, 6xxx/7xxx with grain refiners; Mg-bearing powders), with a sliding interlocked laser guard (OD 7+ window) and a recirculating argon loop with a cyclone and HEPA filter. The machine is meant to sit on a tray of a vertical lift module (Kardex Shuttle) and be tended by a UR12e cobot on a MiR250 mobile base (plate exchange, door, drawer, reservoir swaps).

Please give a sourced, practical safety requirements review a laser safety officer and EHS office would expect, covering: (1) laser: ANSI Z136.1 and Z136.9 (manufacturing), IEC 60825-1 and IEC 60825-4 (guards: passive guard materials and the exposure limits for 500 W at 1070 nm, how long aluminium or steel sheet survives), ISO 11553-1 (laser processing machines), making the machine Class 1 in operation and what changes during service, interlocks (two-channel, guard locking, shutter, safe torque off), viewing windows, beam dumps, back-reflection from aluminium, NHZ, eyewear OD, SOPs and training; (2) inert gas: argon asphyxiation in a small room and inside an enclosed vertical lift module, O2 monitoring and alarm set points (19.5 percent), ventilation, cylinder and regulator safety, over-pressure relief; vacuum and viewport implosion; (3) combustible metal powder: NFPA 484 and NFPA 652 (dust hazard analysis), Kst and MIE of AlSi10Mg and other Al powders, wet versus dry filters, condensate and soot from LPBF filters (pyrophoric filter cake), passivation, vacuums rated for combustible dust, grounding and bonding, PPE and respirators, storage; (4) the heated plate and hot surfaces; (5) the robot and mobile robot: ISO 10218-1/-2:2025, ISO/TS 15066, ANSI/A3 R15.08-1/-2, risk assessment (ISO 12100) for a cobot that reaches into a laser machine; (6) incidents and lessons from LPBF and laser labs (fires, filter fires, powder explosions, laser burns). Where possible, cite university EHS laser safety manuals and lab guidance, and note anything specific to Brigham Young University's published laser safety, compressed gas or combustible dust programs. Give concrete numbers and say clearly where you are estimating.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
The explosive characteristic parameters of additive manufacturing (AM) dust were systematically studied. A systematic experimental study was performed on the characteristic parameters of dust explosions fueled by metal powder for AM, to obtain the distribution pattern of those parameters for four types of AM dust samples. Based on experimental data, the dust-explosive severity was classified via two-dimensional matrix analysis in terms of Pmax and Kst, and the dust-explosive sensitivity was classified via three-dimensional matrix analyses of the MIE, MIT, and MEC. Finally, a dust-explosive risk assessment model of AM metal powder was established based on comprehensive considerations of the dust-explosive severity and sensitivity, and four types of AM dust sample were applied empirically. The risk assessment method can provide a scientifically credible and effective basis for assessing and improving the AM process based on powder spreading.
